text: Lesson 7 introduced dtypes as a quick check to run on any DataFrame. This lesson is about what to actually do once that check tells you something is genuinely wrong.

A CSV column full of numbers can still load as object, Pandas' label for text, for reasons that have nothing to do with the numbers themselves — a stray currency symbol, inconsistent formatting between rows, or a source system that simply quoted every single value as a string on the way out. Pandas ends up treating one-two-zero as three separate characters, not the actual number one hundred twenty.

Here's the actual danger hiding in this: text that merely looks like a number can't be summed the way you'd naturally expect it to be. String addition concatenates the characters together instead of adding the values mathematically, and it does this completely silently — no error message at all, just quietly wrong output that still looks plausible enough at a glance that you might not catch it.

astype converts a column to the actual type it should have been all along. Once converted properly, sum genuinely adds the numbers together — one hundred twenty plus eighty five equals two hundred five — instead of whatever nonsense string concatenation would quietly have handed you instead.

Check dtypes first, always, on absolutely anything freshly loaded into a DataFrame — a numeric-looking column that shows up as object is the single most common data-type surprise you'll run into with real files. Lesson 14 covers a specific, extremely common version of this exact same problem: dates.
